title: “THE JOY OF THE LORD IS YOUR STRENGTH”—BUT WHY DID GOD SAY IT TO PEOPLE WHO WERE CRYING?
paragraphs: “THE JOY OF THE LORD IS YOUR STRENGTH”—BUT WHY DID GOD SAY IT TO PEOPLE WHO WERE CRYING?

Nehemiah 8:10 is one of Christianity’s most quoted promises. But when you discover what happened before those words were spoken, you may never read them the same way again. This was not a command to pretend everything was fine. It was an invitation to receive mercy when the truth about yourself had become almost unbearable.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You wake up. You pray. You smile at people. You answer messages. You go to church. You tell everyone you are blessed.
But somewhere beneath that carefully maintained appearance, something is falling apart.
You still believe in God.
You just don't understand why your heart feels so heavy.
And then somebody tells you, “The joy of the Lord is your strength!”
You nod.
You know the verse.
You've probably heard it preached, sung, printed on coffee mugs, and shared across Facebook a thousand times.
But deep inside, you want to ask a question you are almost ashamed to say out loud.
“What if I don't feel any joy left?”
What if the bills are still unpaid?
What if the marriage is still struggling?
What if the person you prayed for still hasn't come home?
What if your secret sins are haunting you?
What if you have spent so many years pretending to be spiritually strong that you no longer remember what it feels like to be honest with God?
And what if the very Scripture people keep using to tell you to be happy was originally spoken to people who were weeping?
Because it was.
And that changes everything.
In Nehemiah 8, the people of God were not dancing around pretending life was beautiful.
They were crying.
Not because someone had told them a sad story.
Not because they had experienced an emotional worship service.
They were weeping because they had heard the Word of God and realized how far they had wandered from Him.
And right there, in the middle of their tears, came one of the most extraordinary declarations in Scripture.
“The joy of the LORD is your strength.” — Nehemiah 8:10, KJV
But before we rush to claim that promise, we need to stand where those people stood.
We need to hear what they heard.
We need to understand why they cried.
Because the joy that strengthened them was not the shallow happiness of people who had forgotten their sins.
It was the sacred joy of people being invited back into fellowship with the God they had disobeyed.
And perhaps that is exactly the joy your soul has been missing.
Jerusalem had been devastated.

The city had suffered destruction, exile, disgrace, and years of painful rebuilding. The temple had been rebuilt earlier, and under Nehemiah's leadership, the city's walls had finally been restored despite opposition and danger.
But something was still broken.
The walls were standing.
The people were not yet spiritually whole.
And isn't that painfully familiar?
You can rebuild your career and still feel empty.
You can repair your reputation and still carry shame.
You can put your family photographs back on the wall while knowing that something inside your home desperately needs healing.
You can restore everything people see and still have a soul that needs restoration.
Jerusalem had its walls back.
But God's people needed something more than protection from their enemies.
They needed to hear His voice again.
So, in Nehemiah 8, the people gathered in the square before the Water Gate.
Men, women, and all who could understand assembled together.
And they asked Ezra the scribe to bring the Book of the Law of Moses.
Notice that detail.
They asked for the Word.
They were not gathering to hear a motivational speech about their potential.
They were not looking for someone to congratulate them for rebuilding their city.
They wanted to hear what God had said.
Ezra opened the book before the people.
They stood.
He blessed the LORD, the great God.
And the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” lifting their hands before bowing their heads and worshiping with their faces toward the ground.
Then something happened that should challenge every generation of believers.
Nehemiah 8:8 says:
“So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.” — KJV
They did not merely hear religious words.
They were helped to understand them.
The Word was read clearly. Its meaning was explained. The people were brought face-to-face with what God had revealed.
And as understanding entered their minds, conviction entered their hearts.
They began to weep.
Imagine the scene.
A mother standing among the crowd, remembering choices she wished she could undo.
A father hearing God's commands and realizing how often he had failed to lead his household faithfully.
An older man remembering the disobedience that had marked his people.
A young person discovering that the God of Israel was not simply a name inherited from previous generations but the holy, covenant-keeping LORD who deserved wholehearted worship.
Scripture does not record those individual stories. But it does tell us that the people wept when they heard the words of the Law.
And we know enough about the human heart to understand why God's truth can bring us to tears.
Sometimes the hardest moment in your spiritual life is not when somebody exposes your sin.
It is when God opens your eyes and you can no longer excuse it.
You remember the lie.
The bitterness.
The compromise.
The private habit you kept defending.
The person you refused to forgive.
The obedience you kept postponing.
The prayers you spoke publicly while secretly nourishing the very thing you were asking God to deliver you from.
And suddenly, the issue is no longer what everyone else did to you.
It is what you have done before a holy God.
That kind of conviction hurts.
But it can also be the beginning of mercy.
Because God does not expose sin merely to humiliate the sinner.
His Word reveals our condition so that we might turn from sin and return to Him.
Then comes the moment so many people miss.
Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites did not tell the people that their sin was insignificant.
They did not say, “Stop being dramatic.”
They did not announce that holiness no longer mattered.
Instead, they declared that the day was holy to the LORD.
And they instructed the people not to remain in mourning.
Nehemiah 8:9 says the people were weeping when they heard the words of the Law.
Then verse 10 declares:

“Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.” — KJV
Read that again.
God's people had been confronted by His Word.
Their hearts were broken.
And their leaders told them to celebrate.
Why?
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because disobedience had become acceptable.
But because this particular holy day was to be marked by rejoicing before the LORD.
The occasion was the first day of the seventh month, a sacred day of assembly associated with the blowing of trumpets, as described in Leviticus 23:23–25 and Numbers 29:1.
Their tears were understandable, but mourning was not the appointed response for that day.
They were being called to receive God's Word with reverence and to rejoice before Him.
This matters because the Bible does not teach that every holy encounter must end in sorrow.
There is a time to mourn over sin.
There is a time to confess.
There is a time to fast.
And there is also a time to rejoice in the goodness and mercy of God.
In fact, Nehemiah 9 later records a solemn gathering marked by fasting, confession, and worship.
The people were not being taught to avoid repentance.
They were being taught that sorrow was not the whole story of their relationship with God.
Now look at the original Hebrew.
The closing words of Nehemiah 8:10 are:
כִּי־חֶדְוַת יְהוָה הִיא מָעֻזְּכֶם
Ki chedvat Adonai hi ma'uzzekhem.
A careful rendering is:
“For the joy of the LORD is your stronghold.”
The Hebrew word חֶדְוָה (chedvah) means joy or gladness.
The expression חֶדְוַת יְהוָה (chedvat YHWH) is commonly translated “the joy of the LORD.”
The divine name is represented by the four Hebrew consonants יהוה, often written YHWH. “Adonai” is the traditional Jewish reverential reading used in place of pronouncing the divine name.
But there is another word here that deserves our attention.
מָעוֹז (ma'oz) refers to a place or source of strength, a stronghold, refuge, or fortress.
In this verse, מָעֻזְּכֶם (ma'uzzekhem) means “your stronghold” or “your strength.”
And that is remarkable.
Because the people had just rebuilt Jerusalem's physical walls.
Yet they were now being reminded that their deepest security was not found in stone.
It was found in the LORD.
Their city could have walls.
Their homes could have doors.
Their soldiers could carry weapons.
But none of those things could reconcile a sinful people to their holy God.
Their true stronghold was not the structure they had finished building.
It was the LORD in whom they were being called to rejoice.
Do you see the beauty?
They had rebuilt a wall around Jerusalem, but God was teaching them where their real refuge stood.
And perhaps some of us need to hear that tonight.
Your savings are not your ultimate stronghold.
Your job is not your ultimate stronghold.
Your spouse is not your ultimate stronghold.
Your reputation is not your ultimate stronghold.
Even your ability to remain emotionally composed is not your ultimate stronghold.
Those things may be valuable gifts or responsibilities.
But they cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Only God can.
And the joy of the LORD is not something you manufacture by forcing yourself to smile.
It is rooted in who He is, what He has promised, and the goodness of belonging to Him.
There is a meaningful question about the Hebrew expression that deserves careful treatment.
Does “the joy of the LORD” mean the joy God's people experience in Him, or the joy that belongs to God Himself?
The Hebrew construction allows discussion, and interpreters have understood it in more than one way.
In the immediate context, the emphasis falls on the joy associated with the LORD and His holy day, a joy that becomes strength for His people.
Other Scriptures also speak of God's delight in His people, including Zephaniah 3:17.
We should not pretend the grammar alone settles every theological question.
But we can confidently say this:
The joy in Nehemiah 8:10 is God-centered, not circumstance-centered.
It is not a command to deny suffering.
It is not a promise that believers will never experience depression, grief, fear, or exhaustion.
It is not a magical formula guaranteeing that tomorrow will be easier.
It is an invitation to find strength in the LORD rather than allowing sorrow to become the final word.
And that truth becomes even more beautiful when we follow the larger story of Scripture to Jesus Christ.
Because Nehemiah 8 shows a people confronted by the Law.
But the Gospel reveals the Savior to whom the Law ultimately points.
The Law exposes sin.
Christ came to save sinners.
The Law reveals God's righteous standard.
Jesus fulfilled the Law in perfect obedience.
The Law shows us that we cannot justify ourselves before God.
The Gospel announces that sinners can be justified by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
John 1:17 says:
“For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.” — KJV
That does not mean the Law was evil.
It means the Law could not accomplish what only the saving work of Christ could provide.
Paul writes in Romans 3:23:
All.
Not just the person whose scandal became public.
Not just the addict.
Not just the adulterer.
Not just the person who walked away from church.
All.
The pastor needs grace.
The worship leader needs grace.
The person who has memorized hundreds of verses needs grace.
The person reading this article with tears in their eyes needs grace.
And the one writing about grace needs it too.
But Romans does not leave us standing beneath the weight of our guilt.
Romans 3:24 continues:
“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Freely.
By His grace.
Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
There is the heart of the Gospel.
God does not declare sinners righteous because they have successfully hidden their failures.
He justifies those who trust in Jesus Christ because of what Christ has accomplished.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
He bore its judgment.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The cross tells us how seriously God takes sin.
The resurrection tells us that death did not defeat the Savior.
And together, they announce a hope far greater than the temporary relief of pretending everything is fine.
That is why the Gospel does not say, “Your past doesn't matter.”
It says that through Christ, your past does not have to be your master.
It does not say, “You never really sinned.”
It says there is forgiveness for those who repent and believe.
It does not say, “You are strong enough to save yourself.”
It says Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
And maybe that is the word your heart has been waiting to hear.
You do not have to manufacture the strength to become your own redeemer.
You need the Redeemer.
There is a Greek word in the New Testament that helps us see how Christian joy can exist even in suffering.
χαρά (chara) means joy or gladness.
In John 15:11, Jesus says:
“These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.” — KJV
In the Greek text, the expression ἡ χαρὰ ἡ ἐμή (hē chara hē emē) means “my joy.”
Jesus speaks of His joy being in His disciples.
And consider when He spoke these words.
John 15 belongs to Jesus' final teaching to His disciples before His arrest and crucifixion.
The cross was approaching.
Betrayal was approaching.
Suffering was approaching.
And Jesus spoke about joy.
Not because suffering was imaginary.
Not because pain was irrelevant.
But because communion with Him would give His followers a joy deeper than the world's fragile promises.
Jesus never taught His disciples that following Him would eliminate trouble.
In John 16:33, He said:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — KJV
There it is.
Tribulation is real.
Christ's victory is also real.
And His victory is greater.
That means a Christian can weep and still possess hope.
A Christian can be grieving and still belong to Christ.
A Christian can be struggling emotionally and still be held by the grace of God.
Joy is not always expressed through laughter.
Sometimes it is expressed through trembling lips whispering, “Lord, I still trust You.”
Sometimes it is expressed through repentance after years of resistance.
Sometimes it is expressed through opening the Bible again after months of spiritual distance.
Sometimes it is expressed through accepting help instead of continuing to suffer in silence.
Sometimes it is expressed through forgiving someone, while still maintaining wise and necessary boundaries.
And sometimes it is simply the quiet assurance that even though you have no idea what tomorrow will bring, the risen Christ remains faithful.
There is something else in Nehemiah 8:10 that many inspirational quotations leave out.
The people were told to eat, drink, and send portions to those who had nothing prepared.
Don't miss that.
Their celebration was not supposed to become a private spiritual experience disconnected from the needs of others.
Their joy was meant to overflow in generosity.
The person with plenty was to remember the person without.
The household with food was to share with the household that lacked it.
The holy celebration included practical compassion.
This is not an incidental detail.
It reveals something about biblical joy that our generation desperately needs to recover.
Real joy in God does not always make us more comfortable.
It should also make us more compassionate.
When grace has reached your heart, you begin to notice people you once overlooked.
The widow who rarely receives visitors.
The single parent carrying responsibilities nobody sees.
The believer who stopped attending church because shame convinced them they were no longer welcome.
The teenager who seems rebellious but is quietly desperate to know whether anyone would still love them if they told the truth.
The man who looks successful but is one financial emergency away from despair.
The woman who encourages everybody else while privately wondering who will encourage her.
The person who has never opened a Bible because no one has patiently helped them understand it.
Joy in the LORD is not an excuse to ignore their pain.
It is a reason to love them.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
What if you have been asking God to restore your joy while refusing to bring Him the thing that is stealing your peace?
What if the problem is not that God has stopped speaking, but that you have become afraid of what His Word might reveal?
What if you have confused conviction with rejection?
What if you believe that because God is exposing something in your life, He must be preparing to abandon you?
Listen carefully.
Conviction that leads you toward repentance and Christ is not the same as hopeless condemnation.
The enemy of your soul would have you believe that exposure means your story is over.
The Gospel tells us that confession can become the doorway to restoration.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Not because confession earns forgiveness.
Not because tears pay for sin.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
And Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
Notice those final words.
“In Christ Jesus.”
This promise is not permission to remain comfortable in rebellion.
It is the glorious assurance of those who belong to Christ.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
It calls us out of darkness.
It calls us away from the sins that destroy us.
And it brings us into the mercy of the Savior who died and rose again.
You cannot heal by endlessly pretending the wound is not there.
And you cannot grow in holiness by renaming sin as harmless.
But neither can you save yourself by punishing your soul forever.
There is a difference between godly sorrow and hopeless despair.
Second Corinthians 7:10 says:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” — KJV
Godly sorrow turns toward God.
Hopeless despair tells you there is nowhere left to turn.
Godly sorrow confesses.
Despair hides.
Godly sorrow seeks the mercy of Christ.
Despair insists that mercy could never be meant for someone like you.
And perhaps the most dangerous lie you have believed is this:
“Jesus can forgive other people, but He cannot forgive what I have done.”
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the Savior who welcomed repentant sinners, restored fallen disciples, and gave His life for the ungodly.
Your sin is serious.
But you are not being invited to trust in the smallness of your sin.
You are being invited to trust in the greatness of your Savior.
Remember Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then, when fear closed in, he denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine remembering your own voice denying the One you claimed to love.
Luke 22:61 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered the Lord's words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Those were real tears.
His failure was real.
But that was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus spoke with Peter beside the Sea of Tiberias.
Three times, Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's denial did not become something good.
It remained a grievous failure.
But Jesus did not leave Peter trapped inside that failure.
The risen Lord restored him and called him to faithful service.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be celebrated.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ is powerful enough to redeem lives marked by real failure.
And perhaps you need to hear this:
Your worst chapter does not have the authority to overrule the finished work of Jesus Christ.
If you are in Christ, your identity is not ultimately the worst thing you have done.
You are not required to keep living as though the cross never happened.
Repent.
Make things right where you can.
Accept accountability.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible.
Receive the forgiveness God offers in Christ.
And begin walking in obedience again.
This is not cheap grace.
It is costly grace, purchased through the blood of Jesus.
It never gives us permission to cherish sin.
It gives us a reason to leave sin behind.
And now, return with me to that square in Jerusalem.
The people are still standing before Ezra.
The Law has been read.
Their tears have fallen.
They have heard that the day is holy.
They have been instructed to rejoice and share with those who have nothing prepared.
What happens next?
Nehemiah 8:12 tells us:
“And all the people went their way to eat, and to drink, and to send portions, and to make great mirth, because they had understood the words that were declared unto them.” — KJV
Did you catch the reason?
Because they had understood.
Not because their circumstances had suddenly become perfect.
Not because their nation's painful history had been erased.
Not because their responsibilities disappeared.
They rejoiced because they understood what had been declared to them.
Understanding God's Word transformed their response.
And this is why shallow spiritual slogans are never enough.
You do not need someone to keep shouting “Be joyful!” while ignoring the reality of your pain.
You need the truth of God explained faithfully.
You need to know who He is.
You need to understand what He has said.
You need to see how His promises find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
You need a faith that can survive the hospital corridor.
The funeral.
The unanswered question.
The painful confession.
The long season of waiting.
The night when nobody answers your call.
And the morning when you must choose whether to trust God again.
Christian joy is not the absence of every painful emotion.
It is a gift rooted in the God who remains faithful even when life is painful.
It does not mean that faithful Christians never need counseling, medical care, rest, or support from other believers.
Those things are not necessarily signs of weak faith.
God often provides help through the compassion, wisdom, and practical care of others.
And if you are exhausted, please hear this without shame:
You are not commanded to pretend that you are okay.
You are invited to come to Christ truthfully.
He already knows.
He knows what happened.
He knows what you did.
He knows what was done to you.
He knows the prayers you could barely finish.
He knows the temptation you keep battling.
He knows the grief you cannot explain.
And He knows how to meet sinners and sufferers with truth and mercy.
The invitation of Matthew 11:28 remains precious:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — KJV
Jesus did not say, “Come when you have learned how to look strong.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
That is where restoration begins.
Not in your ability to impress God.
But in coming to the Savior who is worthy of your trust.
And if this truth has uncovered something you have been hiding, don't rush past it.
Take a moment.
Not for the sake of an emotional reaction.
Not because tears automatically prove repentance.
But because your soul matters more than maintaining an image.
Ask yourself:
Have I been using Christian language to cover spiritual emptiness?
Have I mistaken busyness in ministry for intimacy with Christ?
Have I been trying to earn God's forgiveness instead of trusting His grace?
Have I become so ashamed of my failures that I no longer believe restoration is possible?
Have I allowed the disappointments of life to convince me that God's goodness has disappeared?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Am I willing to surrender the very thing I keep asking Jesus to heal?
If your heart is answering these questions with tears, you do not have to hide.
You can pray right where you are.

“Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time trying to look stronger than I am. You know the places where I have sinned, the burdens I have carried, and the truth I have been afraid to face. Forgive me. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust Your finished work, and walk in obedience. Restore the joy of knowing You. When my emotions are weak, help me remember that Your faithfulness has not changed. Make me a person who receives Your grace and extends compassion to others. In Your holy name, Amen.”
And if you prayed that sincerely, remember that salvation does not depend on repeating a particular set of words.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, and we are called to repent and believe in Him.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
How many people in your life are quietly living behind a smile?
How many have memorized Nehemiah 8:10 but have never heard the tears that came before it?
How many believe their struggles disqualify them from receiving the mercy of God?
How many have walked away from church because they were wounded, ashamed, confused, or never taught to understand Scripture?
And how many are one compassionate conversation away from opening their hearts to the Gospel again?
Maybe this article was not meant to stop with you.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list needs to read it.
Someone who keeps posting that everything is fine.
Someone who has been spiritually exhausted.
Someone whose past has become a prison.
Someone who believes God is finished with them.
Not merely because it helps a page grow, although it truly helps this ministry reach more people.
Because someone who would never enter a church might still stop to read a testimony of grace.
Because a simple act of sharing could open the door to a conversation about Jesus.
Do it with compassion, not to expose or embarrass them.
And if this message reached a place in your heart that you have struggled to explain, I invite you to comment.
You do not have to share private details or explain everything publicly.
Your words may encourage someone who believes restoration is impossible.
Not as a lucky charm.
Not as a replacement for opening your own Bible.
The people wept.
They heard God's Word.
They were called to rejoice.
They shared with those in need.
And their understanding of the Word shaped their response.
That is worth remembering.
Invite your friends, your children, your parents, your spouse, the believer who is struggling, the person who is searching, and even the skeptic who has questions about Jesus.
This ministry exists to keep pointing people back to Christ through Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, biblical understanding, discipleship, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
We do not want people merely collecting inspirational quotations.
We want people opening their Bibles.
Understanding the context.
Recognizing false teaching.
Growing in holiness.
Learning to pray.
Learning to forgive.
Learning to stand firm when life becomes difficult.
And learning to rejoice in the LORD without pretending that suffering does not exist.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture more deeply, strengthen their walk with Jesus, and grow beyond surface-level inspiration.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
But meaningful ministry requires real resources.
There are materials to prepare, books to develop, discipleship resources to organize, and more people to reach with biblical teaching.
And that brings me to an invitation I want to make with both conviction and transparency.
It is a voluntary act of partnership that helps sustain and expand the work of Gospel Warrior.
It can be part of your personal Christian generosity—an offering of support toward a ministry you believe is faithfully serving others.
But it is important to be biblically clear.
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, worship, love, generosity, and faithful service in the life He has given you.
Supporting a sound Christian ministry can be one meaningful expression of that generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a suggestion that financial support can purchase spiritual favor.
Give freely, thoughtfully, and only as you are able.
You can still pray, share the Gospel, encourage someone, and make use of the free discipleship resources available through this ministry.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth and can also become thoughtful gifts that open conversations about faith.
Come closer to Jesus.
Go deeper into His Word.
Let His truth confront what needs to change.
Let His grace remind you that forgiveness is found in Christ.
And let the joy of the LORD become a source of strength as you follow Him.
Because in the end, Gospel Warrior is not about building an audience that admires a ministry.
It is about pointing people toward a Savior who is worthy of all glory.
And that takes us back to Jerusalem.
Back to the Water Gate.
Back to the people standing beneath the sound of God's Word.
Back to the tears that fell when truth exposed their failures.
And back to the astonishing command to rejoice.
They were not told that sin did not matter.
They were not told that their pain was imaginary.
They were not told that the past had never happened.
They were invited to receive the day God had set before them with holy joy.
And centuries later, we stand on the other side of the cross and the empty tomb, with an even clearer revelation of the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
We know that forgiveness is not wishful thinking.
It was purchased at a terrible price.
We know that death is not the final victor.
Christ is risen.
We know that sinners who come to Him in faith are not required to remain prisoners of their former lives.
And we know that the One who began a good work in His people is faithful to complete it, as Philippians 1:6 teaches.
So when someone tells you, “The joy of the LORD is your strength,” remember the whole story.
Remember the people who cried.
Remember the Word that confronted them.
Remember the holiness of God.
Remember the mercy that called them to rejoice.
Remember the generosity that made room for those who had nothing prepared.
And above all, remember Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest joy of the Christian life is not that everything has gone according to our plans.
It is that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be reconciled to God.
You may still have questions.
You may still have scars.
You may still be rebuilding parts of your life.
And there may be days when your voice shakes as you pray.
But you can turn toward Christ again.
You can confess what needs confessing.
You can seek help where help is needed.
You can obey the next thing God has made clear.
You can open His Word and discover that His truth is not merely meant to be quoted.
It is meant to be understood, believed, and lived.
And if tears come while you read, don't assume that means your faith has failed.
Sometimes tears are part of coming home.
The people of Jerusalem discovered that their tears did not have to be the end of their encounter with God.
Neither do yours.
For the believer, there is a Savior whose mercy is greater than the shame you once thought would define you forever.
A Savior who does not excuse sin but forgives repentant sinners.
A Savior who does not promise a painless life but promises His presence.
A Savior who can take a story marked by failure and make it a testimony to the glory of His grace.
So hold on to the truth.
Not every broken thing is healed overnight.
Not every prayer is answered in the way we expect.
Not every painful consequence disappears.
But Jesus Christ is still worthy of your trust.
And the joy of the LORD remains a stronghold for His people.
You thought your tears meant God was finished with your story. But in Christ, the tears you brought into His presence may become part of the testimony of how His grace brought you home.
